item.title: When Women Don’t Support Women at Work
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

When Women Don’t Support Women at Work

The devastating impact of woman-on-woman hostility in the workplace.

Posted May 1, 2026

Key points
  • Woman-on-woman hostility at work stems from limited opportunities, sparking competition over collaboration.
  • In-group harm cuts like woman-on-woman workplace hostility can cut deeper than systemic sexism.
  • Women leaders can divest from hierarchical systems and facilitate professional ecosystems of interdependence.
Source: Travis Anderson / Pixabay

For decades, the phrase “women supporting women” has circulated as a cultural aspiration invoked in keynote speeches, LinkedIn posts, and corporate mission statements. Yet many women can tell a different story, because the intended culture of a setting often doesn't match the actual climate of that setting. This disparity is particularly harmful when it violates the "women supporting women" ideal.

The organizational culture is the top-down perspective, the set of intentions an organization tries to establish for its workforce. But the workplace climate is the bottom-up perspective—the actual impact of how policies and workplace interactions make people feel.

As a psychologist focused on the importance of systems and relational factors, I am much more interested in the workplace climate than its aspirational culture. I haven't met anyone who has left a job because they disagreed with the organization's stated mission or cultural values. But I have known many people (myself included) who have left jobs because they felt like the mission wasn't actually reflected in workplace encounters, expectations, and norms.

Woman-on-Woman Hostility in the Workplace

With clients, colleagues, and friends, women often commiserate about overt and covert sexism in the workplace. But what is less discussed is that some of the most painful professional wounds are subtle acts from other women. There is an idea that women bosses are better to work for than men, but that certainly isn't always true. It's not always a Devil Wears Prada situation, but the cumulative impact of small instances of women not supporting each other can be emotionally devastating.

So why does this happen? Woman-on-woman workplace hostility is driven largely by the psychological and interpersonal consequences of systems built on scarcity, where women have historically been given only a few seats at the table.

When opportunity is framed as limited, solidarity becomes risky for one's livelihood, and collaboration gets replaced with competition.

Scarcity mindset and resource hoarding undermine the very progress women have fought to achieve. Research consistently shows that organizations with higher levels of female collaboration and mentorship experience better retention, stronger leadership pipelines, and improved organizational performance (Ibarra, Ely, & Kolb, 2013). When women actively sponsor and advocate for one another, they create multiplying effects that extend far beyond individual careers. But the reverse can also be true, and it is not because women are inherently competitive or unsupportive.

Psychologists refer to this as the “queen bee” phenomenon, a pattern in which women who have succeeded in male-dominated environments distance themselves from other women and may even reinforce the same barriers they once faced (Derks, Van Laar, & Ellemers, 2016). Research suggests this behavior often emerges not from hostility but from survival strategies developed in systems that inadvertently teach women that helping other women threatens their own position.

In the vast majority of these situations, the problem isn't really the "queen bee"; it's the "hive" and the generational impact of scarcity mindset and resource insecurity.

Source: Amy (PrettySleepy) / Pixabay

One especially harmful dynamic is managerial mistreatment, which includes behaviors such as public criticism or condescension, withholding support, disparaging performance to others, exclusion from opportunities, and forms of intimidation or retaliation. Research shows that abusive or undermining supervision significantly increases workplace stress, burnout, and psychological distress (Tepper, 2000).

In some cases, this dynamic can escalate into what employees describe as supervisor gaslighting—a pattern in which legitimate concerns are dismissed, experiences are reframed as misunderstandings, or employees are made to question their own competence or perceptions of events. While gaslighting is not a formal clinical diagnosis in organizational psychology, studies of workplace abuse show that manipulative communication from supervisors can destabilize employees’ confidence and increase emotional exhaustion (Hershcovis & Barling, 2010).

When this behavior occurs between women, the impact can be particularly painful, akin to betrayal or abandonment. For women with histories of relational trauma, these experiences can be triggering and deeply destabilizing.

From a relational psychology perspective, this reaction makes sense. Humans are wired for in-group trust. When harm comes from someone we perceive as part of our shared identity, the rupture can feel deeply personal. This dynamic is particularly visible in professions where women have only recently gained authority, including medicine, academia, and mental health fields. Instead of mentorship, younger women sometimes encounter subtle or overt forms of resource hoarding: withheld referrals, guarded knowledge, or exclusion from professional networks.

There is also a psychological cost to the women who engage in gatekeeping. Living in such a defensive posture reinforces the illusion of scarcity that further fuels their anxiety.

Collaboration creates more opportunities than competition

Abundance psychology suggests that when people share opportunities, the network expands, creating more collective success (Covey, 1989). Mentorship, referral networks, collaborative projects, and public advocacy are the mechanisms through which professional ecosystems grow. When those channels close, innovation slows, and burnout accelerates.

The future of women’s leadership depends on shifting this cultural script. Instead of reproducing hierarchical models built on exclusion, women leaders have an opportunity to design professional ecosystems rooted in interdependence. This means openly sharing referrals, mentoring emerging professionals, amplifying one another’s work, and creating collaborative platforms where expertise is distributed rather than guarded.

None of this requires perfection. It requires intentionality and embracing vulnerability.

The truth is that women’s advancement has never been a zero-sum game. But when women replicate scarcity dynamics within their own ranks, everyone loses.

The evidence is clear: When women support one another, industries become more innovative, organizations become more resilient, and leadership becomes more representative of the communities it serves. The most powerful shift we can make is expanding the table rather than defending a single seat. The real measure of leadership is not how high we climb alone, but how many others climb alongside us.

item.title: When Survivors Are Blamed for Family Estrangement
item.description:
Trauma

When Survivors Are Blamed for Family Estrangement

How victim-blaming shows up after family cutoff, and how to respond

Posted May 1, 2026

Key points
  • Survivors of abandonment are often blamed for having been abandoned, shifting the blame off of those who left.
  • Victim-blaming can reinforce shame and distort how abandonment is understood.
  • These prepared responses can help redirect the focus.

Jarelle was in her senior year when she started dating someone outside the family faith. At first, her parents tried to get her to end the relationship, but she refused. She slowly started to draw boundaries with her parents, such as when they could visit and how long they could stay. Over time, they deflected responsibility, blaming everyone but themselves—her partner, her therapist, anyone they believed had “influenced” her. They started distancing themselves and stopped contacting her altogether.

When they didn’t visit after the birth of their first grandchild, their absence was noticeable, but it was the response from others that reinforced the pain she felt.

At first, people asked Jarelle where her parents were and whether they were planning to visit. The questions were uncomfortable, but they made sense. But once her parents cut her off completely, something changed. Instead of wondering about her parents’ absence, others began questioning Jarelle—what had happened, whether she had tried hard enough, and what she might have done to cause the distance.

Jarelle always knew her relationship with her parents was strained, but she held onto the hope that they would show up for important moments. When they didn't, she found herself wondering if their abandonment of her was somehow her fault.

Source: StockSnap / Pixabay

Survivors of abandonment are often blamed for what was done to them

Abandonment doesn’t only happen in childhood—it can also take the form of being cut off or rejected by family in adulthood. Yet when it happens to adults, they are often seen as easier to blame, with the assumption being that they must have caused it. If you can relate to this, keep reading.

Some of this may come from extended family, who may not realize how their statements unintentionally reinforce the behavior of the parent who left. The uncle who urges you to “see it from their perspective,” or a cousin who shouts, “But, she’s your mother!” may not realize the impact of their statement. Some may come from much closer: Siblings or other family members may report feeling “in the middle,” giving equal blame to the victim as the one who abandoned them.

Other statements may come from complete strangers, yet their words may impact you just as much. Insensitive comments online or from mutual friends can come across as blaming you for your abandonment. A social media post about “family is everything,” or a colleague suggesting, “He’s your father. Just give him a call,” shows an overall lack of understanding and lack of compassion for the situation.

article continues after advertisement

Responding to others is only part of the challenge. The other part is internal: the shame, guilt, and self-doubt that can take hold after repeated questioning. Over time, it can become difficult to separate others’ assumptions from your own sense of truth.

When these moments arise, it can help to pause and notice what you’re feeling—whether that’s sadness, anger, relief, or confusion. Naming these reactions can make it easier to respond in a way that doesn't leave you feeling like you have to defend yourself.

You might recognize thoughts like:

  • “When I explain this, it makes me look like the problem.”
  • “Why can’t I just have a normal family?”
  • “Am I overreacting?”

Having go-to responses can help redirect misplaced blame

Many of these comments come from people who do not fully understand the impact of parental abandonment. Their statements may sting, even when they come from a well-meaning place and, perhaps, a lack of understanding.

Of course, there will be some who fully side with or defend the one who abandoned you. These are typically people who have an interest in not seeing the person as having abandoned their child. The parent who left gets a new spouse or has other children, for example, who may be engaged to do the dirty work of defending them. These, in my experience, are the most hurtful and often the most difficult to respond to. However, it may be helpful to see them as having a vested interest in masking the trauma. Unfortunately, this means they have an interest in denying the truth.

article continues after advertisement

In most cases, I recommend not engaging with people who refuse to validate your experience and who choose to deny your reality. However, there may be times when you have to engage with them, such as at extended family gatherings, such as a wedding or a funeral.

For these instances, having a few prepared responses can help reduce the impact of these interactions and prevent you from internalizing misplaced blame.

Here are some I recommend:

  • “I’ve given this a lot of thought, and I no longer wish to blame myself for them leaving.”
  • “Unfortunately, not all families are safe or supportive.”
  • “I’m disappointed as well, but this was their choice.”
  • “I’m focusing on the people who are here and supportive.”

Having some responses ready will not erase the pain of being blamed for your own abandonment, but it can create enough psychological distance to protect your sense of reality—and remind you that responsibility for the relationship ending does not rest with you.

This article is excerpted, in part, from my book Healing From Parental Abandonment and Neglect.

item.title: 3 Ways Good Parents Can Traumatize Their Children
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

3 Ways Good Parents Can Traumatize Their Children

Here's how, despite good intentions, parents can cause inadvertent harm.

Posted May 1, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional neglect can occur even in seemingly healthy families.
  • Emotional presence, not just caregiving, is crucial in parenting.
  • It's repair, not perfection, that truly matters in child-parent attunement.
Source: Kelli McClintock / Unsplash

Many people assume that emotional wounds must come from obviously difficult childhoods filled with abuse, chaos, neglect, or instability. But therapy rooms are also filled with adults who tell a different story. They often describe parents who worked hard, provided financially, and rarely behaved in overtly harmful ways. By most traditional standards, their upbringing was “good.”

Yet these same adults are also more likely to report something harder to name. A lingering feeling of emotional distance, difficulty expressing needs, and a sense that something important was missing, even though nothing was obviously wrong. Psychology has a term that helps explain this paradox: emotional neglect.

Unlike abuse or overt mistreatment, emotional neglect is defined less by what happened and more by what did not happen. Specifically, it refers to the absence of consistent emotional attunement between parent and child. And research suggests that even children raised by well-intentioned, functional parents can experience it.

1. Your Parent Cared, but Didn’t Tune In

Parenting research often distinguishes between caregiving and emotional attunement. Caregiving involves meeting a child’s physical and logistical needs: food, shelter, safety, and schooling. Attunement, on the other hand, involves recognizing and responding to a child’s internal emotional world.

Developmental psychologist Edward Tronick demonstrated the importance of this connection in his famous “still face experiment.” In the experiment, infants interacted normally with their mothers until the mother suddenly adopted a neutral, unresponsive expression. Within seconds, babies became distressed, attempting repeatedly to re-engage their caregiver. When the lack of response continued, many infants showed signs of emotional withdrawal.

The lesson from this research is not that parents must be perfectly responsive. In fact, Tronick’s later work emphasizes that brief mismatches between parent and child are normal. What matters is repair. Healthy relationships involve cycles of misattunement followed by reconnection.

But when emotional responsiveness is consistently limited, children may learn that their inner experiences are not particularly important or safe to express.

2. Your Parent Didn’t Give Any Emotional Feedback

The phrase “good enough parent” was originally coined by psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott to describe caregivers who meet children’s needs without striving for unrealistic perfection. According to Winnicott, children benefit from parents who are generally responsive but allow manageable frustrations that promote independence.

However, the concept is often misunderstood. Being good enough does not simply mean avoiding harm; it also requires emotional presence. In modern families, many parents successfully meet practical demands but struggle with emotional availability. Work stress, cultural expectations, mental health challenges, and digital distraction can all interfere with attuned interaction.

article continues after advertisement

From the outside, these families often appear healthy. The child attends school, receives support, and avoids major conflict, yet subtle emotional gaps may persist. Emotional neglect may be particularly difficult for adults to recognize because it lacks clear memories of negative events.

A large body of work on adverse childhood experiences shows that overt abuse predicts later mental health difficulties. But studies also show that emotional neglect independently predicts depression, anxiety, and difficulties with emotional regulation.

One reason is that emotional neglect affects how children learn to understand their own feelings. Developmental research indicates that children rely on caregivers to help label and regulate emotions. When a parent responds to distress with curiosity and validation, children gradually internalize those regulatory skills. When that feedback is absent, children may struggle to identify or trust their own emotional signals.

This process is sometimes described as a deficit in “emotional mirroring.” Without consistent mirroring, children may grow up feeling disconnected from their internal experiences.

3. Your Parent Was Affectionate, but Not Consistent

Attachment theory provides another lens for understanding why emotionally adequate households can still produce emotional deprivation.

Research by Mary Ainsworth and later attachment scholars shows that secure attachment develops when caregivers respond consistently and sensitively to a child’s emotional cues. But when caregivers are distant or inconsistent, children may develop avoidant or anxious attachment patterns.

Importantly, these patterns do not necessarily emerge from overtly negative parenting. A caregiver can be responsible and loving while still being emotionally reserved or uncomfortable with emotional expression.

Children raised in such environments often adapt by minimizing their own needs. This can look like maturity or independence in childhood. But in adulthood, it may manifest as difficulty asking for support, discomfort with vulnerability, or a chronic sense of loneliness.

And this is another reason why emotional deprivation can go unnoticed: its effects often emerge gradually.

Children are remarkably adaptive. When emotional needs are not fully met, they frequently adjust their expectations rather than challenge the environment. This allows them to maintain a sense of stability within the family. But those adaptations can become limiting in adulthood.

For example, individuals who learned to suppress emotional needs may struggle to identify what they want in relationships. Others may become highly self-sufficient but feel uncomfortable depending on others. Some develop strong external competence while privately experiencing emotional emptiness.

article continues after advertisement

Recognizing the Invisible ‘Parenting’ Gap

One challenge for adults raised in these circumstances is that acknowledging emotional deprivation can feel like disloyalty. Many of us genuinely respect and appreciate our parents’ efforts. However, recognizing unmet emotional needs does not mean those parents failed or did not care. Instead, it reflects a broader understanding of how human emotional development works.

Parenting occurs within cultural, economic, and personal constraints. Many caregivers were themselves raised in environments where emotional expression was discouraged. They may have provided the best version of care they knew.

Understanding this context allows adult children to hold two truths simultaneously. Their parents may have done their best. And something meaningful may still have been missing. The encouraging news is that emotional development does not stop in childhood.

Secure relational patterns can develop later in life through corrective emotional experiences. Close friendships, supportive romantic relationships, and therapy can all provide opportunities to practice emotional awareness and connection. Psychological interventions that focus on emotion identification and regulation have also shown strong outcomes for individuals who struggle with emotional clarity.

Perhaps most importantly, simply naming the experience of emotional neglect can be transformative. When people recognize that their feelings of emptiness have a developmental context, those feelings often become easier to understand and address.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: When It’s Not Erectile Dysfunction
item.description:
Sex

When It’s Not Erectile Dysfunction

How normal erectile variability gets mistaken for a diagnosis.

Posted May 1, 2026

Key points
  • Erectile disorder has a specific clinical definition that men with erection difficulty do always not meet.
  • Variability in erections is normal and not necessarily a dysfunction.
  • Excessive worry about erections is a common way men inadvertantly contribute to erectile issues.
Source: cottonbro studio / Pexels

Erectile dysfunction (ED) is a real problem, affecting millions of men worldwide. It is also one of the most over-applied terms in men's health. This is especially the case when we self-diagnose.

If you're experiencing difficulty with erections for the first time, you might wonder: Do I have ED?

Probably not. Understanding the difference between dysfunction and normal variability matters more than you might think.

Please note that the following case is a composite with client details anonymized to protect privacy.

Mark was 28 years old and relatively fresh out of his first and only relationship—a high school romance. He had never experienced erectile problems during the relationship, but the couple had also stopped having any kind of intimacy over the past few years. He denied anxiety about being single and was actively looking forward to dating again. However, several of his first new sexual encounters ended with an unexpected outcome—difficulty maintaining his erections.

He entered therapy talking about his problems with “erectile dysfunction.” But was this term accurate?

The Clinical Definition

Erectile dysfunction requires meeting a specific clinical threshold. According to the DSM-5, an erectile disorder is when you experience difficulty getting or maintaining an erection (or have a noticeable change in rigidity) during at least 75 percent of sexual activity for at least six months.

That's a high bar. And it's intentional. When any erection difficulty gets labeled as ED, it’s not clinically accurate and creates unnecessary stigma.

Mark was worried that his erection problems were part of a larger issue—that this was the start of a downhill slide and the rest of his sexual life would be plagued with trouble. At the same time, he acknowledged he had no issues when masturbating on his own. Even during partnered sex, his erections were not completely unreliable. Sometimes, he had no trouble. Other times, his erections would return during an encounter. He did not meet the “75 percent of sexual activity” criteria.

When It's Not ED

Losing an erection after a night of drinking is not ED. Going soft while in conflict with a partner is not ED. Having difficulty shortly after orgasm is not ED.

Erections naturally fluctuate. This is true at any age and becomes more noticeable as we get older. Many physical and psychological factors can contribute to erection variability: alcohol, poor sleep, stress, dehydration, anxiety, relationship tension, and refractory periods. These are all normal.

These types of difficulty do not require ED treatment. They require context. When situational factors can be identified and addressed, it helps switch the focus away from thinking of yourself as “broken.”

In fact, one of the most common ways men develop genuine erectile dysfunction is by excessively worrying. When a man begins monitoring his erections, anxiety builds, causing disconnection during sex, and reinforcing the belief that sex is difficult. This then leads to an avoidance of intimacy, making any future encounters more intimidating. This is performance pressure feeding upon itself.

When the cause of his erection issues was uncertain, Mark blamed himself. He focused on his faults and, during sexual encounters, looked for signs that he was “failing.” This distracted him from what was pleasurable in those moments.

Through therapy, Mark was able to identify an important commonality in the times he had erection trouble—usually it was with a partner he did not know very well, when he pushed himself to have sex sooner than he was ready.

A Problem With the Word "Dysfunction"

Even when erection difficulties are persistent enough to meet clinical criteria, the word dysfunction tells an incomplete story.

In most cases, some function remains. A man may have difficulty with a partner but no problem when alone. He may experience arousal and partial erections without full rigidity. He may get hard for some period of time.

That's function. It matters because where we focus our attention shapes our experience. When the negative absorbs our attention, we feel discouraged and hopeless. When we consider what's going right, we create room for progress.

No one’s anxiety is going to turn off like a light switch. Although Mark wanted that exact outcome, he instead learned how to accept his body as it showed up and navigate his anxiety in a new way. It was true that when he waited a few dates before having sex with a new partner, he felt more comfortable and had fewer erectile issues. And, even when he did experience normal variability, he was able to take it in stride, stay connected to his partner, and focus on other forms of pleasure.

This is a simple and important fact: Even with significant erectile difficulty, men can still reach orgasm and ejaculation. More importantly, they can experience intimacy, connection, and pleasure. Those are not consolation prizes. They are the foundation of a satisfying sex life.

When to Seek Help

You don't have to meet the clinical threshold for ED to deserve support. If you experience changes with your erections and they’re bothering you, that's enough of a reason to talk to someone.

If erection difficulties are persistent, distressing, or affecting your relationship, seek help. Effective treatments exist—both medical and psychological. Regardless if you are experiencing an erectile disorder or just an unexpected variation, know that you are having a normal experience, and you don’t have to go through it alone.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: When Disappointment Wrecks You, Here's What to Do
item.description:
Mindfulness

When Disappointment Wrecks You, Here's What to Do

Everyone feels disappointment. Fortunately, mindfulness can transform it.

Posted May 1, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that mindfulness increases tolerance for emotional distress.
  • Greater acceptance of events alters how one views their own expectations.
  • An effective mindfulness practice for transforming disappointment begins with awareness and breath.
Source: kinga-cichewicz / Unsplash

Your friend who is meeting you on Friday or Saturday cancels on you at the last minute. The successful project you completed at work was not appreciated. One of your best friends totally forgets your birthday. Or, maybe you came in second in a competition. Have any of these things ever happened to you?

Join the club. It would be rare if you had never experienced these and countless other forms of disappointment.

Let me share a personal example of disappointment. I had a recent birthday and got a gift that a family member sent to me. It was a fountain that was perfect for my office. I got batteries, filled the reservoir with water, and turned on the little switch hidden in the back.

In anticipation, I waited for cascading water to dance over the river rocks. And waited. And waited some more. But not a sputter or gurgle came out. Nada.

After shaking, cajoling, and adjusting the water levels, I had to admit the inevitable—this fountain was defective. In that moment, I felt real disappointment. The fountain didn’t cascade, but my mind cascaded with several worrisome thoughts: “Where do I find this store in Portland?” “What if they don’t let me return the fountain?” “I’m very busy—I don’t have time to drive there and twiddle my thumbs in the customer return line.” I noticed these thoughts in the moment, surprised by how quickly they bubbled up from my mind.

In that moment, I consciously countered these thoughts with more likely and soothing thoughts like: “I’m sure they have a return policy—and I have the receipt.” "These things happen, and maybe I could enjoy a trip out of the office on a nice day like today.”

As you may imagine, my disappointment over the faulty fountain didn’t last very long. Of course, this is easier to do when it’s an inanimate object like a fountain that is doing the disappointment. A fountain can’t reject you. It can’t criticize you unfairly. It can’t judge you in any way. Disappointment is a natural feeling. And there will always be some disappointment in life. Sigh.

Use Mindfulness to Overcome Disappointment

Research shows that mindfulness can increase tolerance for distress--whether from disappointment, loss, or other challenges. You might think of this as a kind of resilience that helps you to accept and tolerate outcomes that are vastly different from your expectations. This means that your expectations don't have to be met just the way you want. This broadening of your mental approach makes you freer, more accepting, and less likely to deflate when your best laid plans go awry. When you are more accepting of outcomes, that basically means that you are rewiring your brain so that you don't have to take any outcome personally.

article continues after advertisement

Let me share a mindfulness approach to reframing your experience. These and other tools for overcoming obstacles are in my book, Simply Mindful Resilience. When something occurs that starts to tie you in knots of disappointment, begin by reminding yourself that everyone is trying to do their best, even though it might not be what you want. And that's okay.

When a disappointment comes, start noticing the thoughts you have about the disappointment. Being aware of your thoughts and feelings gives you a moment to slow down and pause. You are simply witnessing the thoughts like a detective who is searching for clues. Take a nice breath, and as you exhale slowly, imagine that you are letting all those initial and often pre-programmed thoughts go. By releasing them, you have created the space necessary to counter and reframe those negative thoughts with more soothing ones.

Conclusion

You may discover that this practice takes only a minute or two. What's important is that you practice it each time your expectations are unmet. After a while, you might find this practice can be as soothing for you as the sound of a burbling brook... speaking of which, remember the fountain that didn't work? Well, they didn’t have the fountain in stock, so I got a much-needed appliance instead.

item.title: What Is a Human Worth?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

What Is a Human Worth?

Labour Day 2026 should be considered a day of value reckoning.

Posted May 1, 2026

Key points
  • AI decouples economic value from human contribution, intensifying jobless growth.
  • AI cannot replace human empathy, judgment, or care, which are crucial but often undervalued economically.
  • A quadruple bottom line—purpose, people, profit, planet—redefines success, beyond just ROI.

Let’s start with a number that should reframe, not calm, the AI conversation. According to the ILO Employment and Social Trends 2026, 408 million people globally want paid work and cannot get it. The “jobs gap” goes far beyond unemployment; it includes the discouraged, the underemployed, and those who stopped looking. More than the entire population of the United States is, today, economically stranded.

And yet the dominant narrative around AI is one of reassurance: Automation will create more jobs than it destroys, systems will augment rather than replace, and disruption will be temporary. The tone suggests control. The data suggests drift.

AI is amplifying an already fragile one. The same ILO analysis of labour underutilization makes clear that traditional unemployment metrics underestimate reality; the gap between those who count and those who matter is widening.

What AI accelerates is not simply task automation. It accelerates a deeper shift: the decoupling of economic value from human contribution. Growth without jobs is no longer a warning sign—it is becoming a structural feature. Even the ILO notes that AI and automation could intensify pressures, particularly for those entering the labour market with skills that may no longer map cleanly onto demand.

May Day 2026 unfolds in unsettled political weather. Tariff walls rise. The US–China tech split deepens. Supply chains reroute, then reroute again. Fossil fuel use is going up while planetary health is in steady decline. Real wages still lag behind inflation shocks, and the pathways that once integrated workers into the global economy are losing momentum. Stability in headline unemployment obscures instability in lived experience.

So the question behind the numbers sharpens. Not how many jobs AI will create.
But what, and who, we still choose to value. So here we are. Happy hybrid Labour Day.

A wrong value orientation

The strange thing about this moment is that the things AI genuinely cannot do—the things that remain stubbornly, exasperatingly human—are the things we have never figured out how to pay for properly.

The nurse who remembers which patient is afraid of silence. The teacher who reads the particular flatness in a teenager's eyes and decides today is not the day for the curriculum. The mediator who holds a room together not because she has the best argument, but because people trust her body in the space. These capacities are not skills in the sense that we measure skill sets. They are something closer to a way of being, accrued through friction, failure, and time.

Artificial intelligence is truly extraordinary at a great many things. Synthesis. Pattern recognition. Speed. Consistency that no human could sustain across a million iterations. But it is not in the room in any meaningful sense. It does not have skin in the game. It has no stake in whether you thrive. And the older one gets—or rather, the longer one watches how humans actually navigate (around) each other—the more convinced one becomes that this distinction matters enormously, and the more puzzled one is by how little our economic frameworks account for it.

article continues after advertisement

Our narrow lens

Here is the fundamental problem. The primary lens through which institutions, companies, and governments evaluate human work is return on investment. ROI. A ratio. Tidy, portable, universally legible. And when applied to humans, completely insufficient.

It is not that profit doesn't matter. Of course it does. Organisations that can't sustain themselves financially can't sustain anything else either. But treating ROI as the singular measure of whether something is working is like navigating a city using only one street. You will find some destinations. You will miss others entirely. And some of what you miss will turn out to be load-bearing.

What we need—and this is less a utopian proposition than a practical one—is something like a Quadruple Bottomline. Purpose, people, profit, planet. Each is held accountable. Each measured. The organisation that posts extraordinary quarterly returns while hollowing out its workforce, exhausting its communities, and externalising its environmental costs is not succeeding. It is borrowing. And at some point, the bill comes.

This is what hybrid development actually means, if you strip away the jargon. Designing economies and institutions that treat natural intelligence and artificial intelligence as complementary. They must not be locked in a zero-sum race where one replaces the other. They can be orchestrated in ways that make them organically interwoven in a modus where each does what it is actually suited for. Machine speed and scale. Human judgment, care, context. The bet is that the combination is greater than either alone. There is evidence for this. The harder question is whether our incentive structures will allow us to pursue it.

The geopolitics that complicate everything

The Global South in 2026 faces a particular squeeze. Demographic growth is producing enormous young workforces at exactly the moment the traditional routes—export manufacturing, trade-linked formalisation—are closing off through automation and reshoring. In low-income countries, new jobs are growing by 3.1 percent, but weak productivity gains and limited structural transformation mean most of them are of low quality.

article continues after advertisement

What gets missed in most AI governance conversations is that countries like Morocco, Malaysia, or Mauritania are far more than navigating a technology transition. They are navigating a civilisational choice about what kind of development path they want and on whose terms. The frameworks being handed down from wealthier countries were not designed with their populations in mind. A ProSocial AI approach—building and governing AI systems around measurable human and social benefit, with planetary dignity, moves beyond efficiency gains. But that is not altruism. It is the foundation of any AI policy that will actually hold in a hybrid world in which millions are still left behind.

The practical argument points toward what might be called double literacy. Two strands, both necessary. First, human literacy: understanding and actively cultivating what natural human intelligence actually does—compassion, creativity, embodied judgment, the slow wisdom that comes from living a life. Second, algorithmic literacy: understanding how AI systems work well enough to engage them critically—to spot where they fail, whose values they encode, and when to override them.

A society that develops only the second strand produces technically fluent people who have misplaced the question of what they are optimising for. A society that ignores the second produces people who are simply not equipped for the world they are living in. Both gaps are real. Both are expensive.

A practical takeaway for May Day 2026

Pick one decision you are making—a hire, a contract, a curriculum, a procurement—and run it through all four columns: purpose, people, profit, planet. As a genuine reckoning. See what shows up in the columns you usually skip.

It will feel unfamiliar. Maybe even a little uncomfortable, the first few times. That is the friction of developing a habit of attention that the dominant economic grammar has been actively discouraging for decades.

But that friction is the point. Outsourcing it is always an option. Understanding what it costs when you do — that is what it means to be human in 2026, and to mean it.
